claims.claim: Online age-checking laws usually use eighteen or another legislatively specified age as the threshold.
Institutions are especially likely to expand an existing access-control mechanism once they discover that it exists.
Age-checking systems can expand into identity infrastructure through institutional incentives without a coordinated plan.
Services may find a token already accepted by another service attractive for adoption.
An agency overseeing age-check compliance may seek audit trails that more clearly record whether checks occurred.
Reusing age-checking infrastructure can reduce integration costs.
More extensive age-checking records or shared infrastructure can make enforcement easier.
Shared age-checking infrastructure can reduce duplication among systems.
A series of individually practical expansions of age checking can collectively produce a common credential layer.
A credential repository or verification system becomes more valuable as more services depend on it.
The consequences of credential-system errors increase as the credential is used for more purposes or services.
Privacy-preserving design can reduce some risks created by online age-checking systems.
Access to ordinary online life is likely to become conditioned on carrying an approved credential when age-checking systems are deployed.
Technical data minimization limits the information revealed by an individual age check.
Technical data minimization does not prevent an age-checking mechanism from being adopted for additional uses or services.
Once a credential is normalized as a condition for access to ordinary online speech, its use will expand beyond the narrow scope stated in its authorizing statute.
